note: The ONLY place two differently-spelled names in this domain may become one person, in data/research/newspapers/identity.json's shape and under its rules: a merge needs a rule, the rule names BOTH spellings verbatim, and a surname-only merge is always a refusal. A refusal is declared as explicitly as a merge — the absence of one reads like a pair nobody has looked at yet.

The chapter names four Chicago men in a bare-surname list — 'Hubbard, Beaubien, Crafts and the Kinzies' — and then names three of them in full further down; the merges rest on the full namings and never on the list.

passes.what: Every person named in The Autobiography of Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard (1911) at the pages declared in coverage.json, ruled against this project's own residents. THE BOOK'S PEOPLE ARE MOSTLY NOT THE SCENE YEAR'S PEOPLE and that is the first thing this pass established: Hubbard's own narrative stops in November 1830, so almost every name he prints is named for something done between 1812 and 1830. The 1830-1836 namings are concentrated in two places — the town-trustee list of 11 August 1834 and the 1835 material — and both are Caroline McIlvaine's 1911 Introduction, not Hubbard.
passes.detail: In this file. THE COUNT THE TICKET ASKS FOR: 35 distinct persons are named across the 92 claims. Seven are merged, fifteen are refused, two match this project's spelling exactly and need no merge (J. K. Boyer at bk_hub_026 against data/residents/households/hh_placed_j_k_boyer.json, and Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard on the title page, already merged into by T-0575 and not re-declared here). The remaining eleven are named for events wholly outside this town — Deschamps, Ramsey Crooks, Warner, Bieson, Beebeau, Bourbonais, Hall, Jombeau, Vasseur, Portier and Dominick Bray, all of them Illinois River and Mackinaw men — and are recorded here as examined and unmatched rather than ruled on one by one, because none of them is ever placed at Chicago by the source.

passes.ruled_on: The rulings are anchored to bk_hub_026 (the town trustees of 11 August 1834), bk_hub_016 and bk_hub_031 (the 1835 arrivals and the 1835 land purchase), bk_hub_040, bk_hub_041, bk_hub_048, bk_hub_049 and bk_hub_094 (the Kinzie household), bk_hub_065 (Beaubien after Craft), bk_hub_090 (Wolcott and Heacock in the fort), bk_hub_097 (Caldwell and Shaub-e-nee) and bk_hub_102 (Caldwell in November 1830). The other claims name no person to rule on, or name one already ruled on: that is not a shortfall, it is what a book of landscape, buildings and river mouths looks like.

passes.what: Every person named in leaves 1-429 of Fergus' Historical Series Nos. 26-29 whose naming falls in the 1830-1836 window, against this project's residents, voters and letter-list names. THE WINDOW IS WHAT MAKES THIS PASS SMALL. The half holds hundreds of names and almost all of them are outside it: No. 26's chiefs speak in 1811, No. 27's are dead or removed before the plat, and No. 28's officer, church and society lists are 1843 lists of 1843 men. Five names fall inside, and all five are ruled on here.
passes.outside_the_window: Robert Fergus (a resident from 1 July 1839, four years after the scene, and the compiler rather than a subject); James W. Norris (canvassed in 1843); William Ellis (printing in 1843-44); Sidney Abell (postmaster from 1837); William Stuart (postmaster in 1843); Alson S. Sherman, Mark Skinner, William Jones, Silas Meacham, George W. Meeker and John B. Weir and the rest of the 1843 society and company officers; Capt. John Whistler (built the first fort in 1803); To-pen-ne-bec, Oseemit, Five Medals, White Loon, Little Turtle, Me-te-a and William Wells (1811-1812); Major Daniel W. Beckwith (surveying on the Kankakee in May 1834 - inside the window by date and outside it by place, and he is not claimed as a Chicago man here); Henry R. Schoolcraft (at Chicago in August 1821). NONE OF THESE WAS CROSSWALKED AND NONE IS A HOLE: a name outside the window is not a candidate, and saying so here is what keeps the next sweep from doing the work again.
passes.note: Two of the five inside the window are the same men this project already holds, and one of the two - Hogan - is corroborated in a way the resident record did not carry: it says Chicago's mail began in his store, and Fergus dates his postmastership and names the man before him.

The pass is small because the half is mostly 1843 and mostly Jacksonville: Fergus No. 28 is a directory of a town eight years past the scene, and Fergus No. 29 is a Morgan County family memoir. Only the Obituary and Robert Fergus's bracketed annotations name anybody inside the window at all.

merges.rule: Hurlbut's chapter names 'Gurdon S. Hubbard, Esq. then a youth of sixteen', born Windsor, Vt., 1802, who first arrived at Chicago at the end of October 1818 and in 1828 bought the American Fur Company's entire interest in the trade of Illinois. This project's resident record is Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard, graded attested. Three things agree and the surname is the least of them: the given name plus middle initial, where Gurdon S. Hubbard is Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard initial for initial and Gurdon is not a common given name; the town, both being at Chicago; and the TRADE, where the resident record's own occupation note already says he 'supplied Andreas with the Ramsey Crooks correspondence on the early fur trade' and Ramsey Crooks is named on this same page as the company's western manager. A common-name coincidence does not reach three agreements, and there was one Gurdon Hubbard at Chicago.
evidence: data/residents/households/hh_hubbard_gurdon.json — persons[0] (hubbard_gurdon, Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard, occupation packer, attested)
data/residents/households/hh_hubbard_gurdon.json — the occupation note naming the Ramsey Crooks correspondence on the early fur trade
merges.does_not_follow: NOTHING IN data/residents/ IS EDITED BY THIS MERGE, and one thing it argues for is deliberately left undone. hh_hubbard_gurdon.json grades his arrival year 1818 RECONSTRUCTED and says 'the year could not be traced to a sentence here, so it is carried as a conjecture citing nothing and flagged for a later parcel to fix or delete'; bk_afc_004 is a sentence, and it gives the day. Making that change is a resident-record edit and a second demonstration, so it is proposed in T-0575 and carries its own ticket rather than being smuggled into a reading pass.

merges.rule: Hurlbut's chapter says the American Fur Company 'transferred Jean Baptiste Beaubien from Milwaukee to this point' in the autumn of 1819, and its bracketed note on a later outfit entry calls the same man 'The late Col. J.B. Beaubien, of Chicago'. This project's resident record is Col. Jean Baptiste Beaubien, graded attested. The full given names and surname agree exactly, the title Col. agrees, and two independent attributes agree with the resident record's own sourced notes: MILWAUKEE, where hh_beaubien_jean_baptiste.json carries 'He was settled as a trader in Milwaukee as early as 1800, and until 1818 had a trading-house there' out of Andreas, and the COMPANY, where the same record's occupation note already says he was 'before that the American Fur Company's man at Chicago'. Andreas and Hurlbut are not copies of each other and both say a Jean Baptiste Beaubien came from the Milwaukee trade to Chicago for that company.
evidence: data/residents/households/hh_beaubien_jean_baptiste.json — persons[0] (beaubien_jean_baptiste, Col. Jean Baptiste Beaubien, occupation trader, attested)
data/residents/households/hh_beaubien_jean_baptiste.json — origin 'Detroit and the Milwaukee trade', attested, sourced andreas_1884_v1
merges.does_not_follow: NOTHING IN data/structures/ IS EDITED BY THIS MERGE. bk_afc_009 says the house Beaubien moved his family into in 1822 was the United States Factory House, bought from the government and standing just south of Fort Dearborn — which is what this project models as jb_beaubien_homestead. That is an origin for a building record and it is a claim of 1822 about a scene of 1835, so it is proposed in T-0575 for docs/RESEARCH/jb_beaubien_homestead.md and not written into the structure here. The 1819 trading houses at the old river mouth by the foot of Harrison Street are a different building again, sixteen years and one harbour cut earlier, and nothing is drawn from them.

merges.rule: The American Fur Company's outfit book of 1821 reads 'Consignment to address of Jamie Kinzie for account of him and the American Fur Company; for trade of Milliwaki, to Chicago', and Hurlbut's own bracketed note immediately under it reads 'The late James Kinzie, formerly of Chicago, and half brother of the late John H. Kinzie.' The merge of Jamie Kinzie into James Kinzie is therefore not this project's inference at all: it is the editor's identification, printed on the page beside the entry it explains, and Jamie is the familiar form of James. It carries to this project's resident James Kinzie on the town — 'formerly of Chicago' — and on the kinship, this dataset holding John Harris Kinzie as a separate resident under the name Hurlbut abbreviates to John H. Kinzie.
evidence: data/residents/households/hh_kinzie_james.json — persons[0] (kinzie_james, James Kinzie, occupation merchant, attested)
data/residents/households/hh_kinzie_john_h.json — persons[0] (kinzie_john_h, John Harris Kinzie, attested), the man Hurlbut's note names as the half brother
merges.does_not_follow: The KINSHIP is not written into either household record on this ticket. Hurlbut says half brother, which is a specific and easily-flattened relationship, and adding a family link between two existing households is a change to the residents dataset rather than a reading of a book. It is recorded in bk_afc_015 and proposed in T-0575. Nor does a consignment addressed to a man in 1821 put him anywhere in 1835: hh_kinzie_james.json already dates his arrival from the 1831 ferry bond and this reading does not move it.

merges.rule: Hurlbut's chapter reads 'Mr. John Crafts was a trader sent to Chicago by a Mr. Conant, of Detroit' and, three sentences on, 'Crafts died here of bilious fever in December, of I think the year 1823.' Fergus's obituary of the old settlers prints 'Crafts, John, died 1825.', read into this project as fdn0137 with the normalized name John Crafts. Given name and surname agree in full; both are men named John Crafts who died at Chicago; and both are placed in the town's first trading generation, one by the American Fur Company narrative and the other by inclusion in a list of Chicago's old settlers. Chicago in the early 1820s held a few dozen households and did not hold two John Craftses.
merges.does_not_follow: THE TWO DEATH YEARS ARE NOT RECONCILED AND THIS MERGE DOES NOT PICK ONE. Hubbard says December, 'I think the year 1823', with the hedge in the source's own words; Fergus's printed list says 1825. Both readings stand as filed, the disagreement is the finding, and choosing between them would be inventing a certainty neither source offers. Nothing follows for the town either way: John Crafts was dead at least ten years before the scene date, he is in no resident record, and none is created.

merges.rule: Caroline M. McIlvaine's Introduction calls him 'Gurdon Hubbard' throughout — 'In 1834 Gurdon Hubbard went to Chicago to remain for the rest of his life' — while the title page of the same volume prints Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard, and this project's resident record is Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard, graded attested. The merge rests on the volume itself and not on a surname: one book, one man, two spellings of him between its covers, with the fuller form on its own title page. Gurdon is not a common given name and the Introduction is explicitly about the subject of the Autobiography.
evidence: the title page of the volume, read at leaf 15 of data/research/books/text/hubbard_autobiography_1911.txt
merges.does_not_follow: It does not follow that anything McIlvaine says about him in 1835 is eyewitness. She is writing in 1911 and Hubbard's own narrative ends in November 1830 (bk_hub_104).

merges.rule: Hubbard writes 'John H. Kinzie' of the Mackinaw clerk of about his own age whose father then resided at Chicago and who gave him letters of introduction to the family. This project's resident record is John Harris Kinzie, graded attested, whose own 1834 advertisement is for 'J. H. Kinzie, forwarding and commission merchant' and who had been Indian sub-agent at Fort Winnebago. Given name, middle initial and surname agree initial for initial; the father at Chicago agrees; and John H. Kinzie is how the man signed himself. A surname alone would be refused here and this is not one.
merges.does_not_follow: It does not follow that he was at Chicago in 1818. Hubbard is explicit that John H. Kinzie 'was stationed permanently at Mackinaw, and was not to be sent into the Indian country'.

merges.rule: Hubbard names 'Robert Kinzie' twice: as 'their youngest son, Robert, late paymaster of the U. S. Army' among the family he met in 1818, and as the man who rose with him and swam the river to the fort fire. This project's resident record is Robert Allen Kinzie, graded attested, named in the 1833 roster as one of 'The Kinzies, John and Robert A., merchants' and recorded by Andreas as the one who remained in Chicago when the rest of the family left in the spring of 1831. Given name plus the same household plus the same generation; the middle name is supplied by this project's record and not contradicted by the book.
merges.does_not_follow: It does not follow that he is placed anywhere in 1835 by this source. Both namings are 1818 and 1827.

merges.rule: The book prints 'Russell E. Heacock' as one of two American families occupying the old log officers' quarters inside the pickets of the ungarrisoned fort in July 1827. This project's resident record is Russel E. Heacock, graded attested, an attorney and justice of the peace who Andreas says 'had come in 1827'. The two spellings differ by one letter in the surname and agree in given name, middle initial and surname otherwise; the arrival year in this project's own record is the year of the book's naming. The one-l and two-l spellings of this surname are both in nineteenth-century print.
merges.does_not_follow: It does not follow that his 1835 dwelling was in the fort. The naming is July 1827, when the fort had no garrison; by 1835 it had.

merges.rule: McIlvaine's list of the town trustees chosen at the election of 11 August 1834 names 'J. S. C. Hogan'. This project's resident record is John S. C. Hogan, graded attested — 'John S. C. Hogan, Postmaster, came in 1832'. Three initials and a surname against a given name and the same three-part sequence, in the same town, in a civic list two years after this project's own record has him arriving. Initials plus a surname would be a refusal if the initials were two; three initials in the same order against the same surname, in a printed list of five trustees, is a match.
merges.does_not_follow: It does not follow that this project may now grade him a trustee. The list is McIlvaine's, written in 1911, and belongs beside the town's own record of the 1834 election and not in front of it.

merges.rule: Hubbard writes that the American Fur Company's round-log storehouse on the river edge, built and occupied by its agent Mr John Craft, 'after the death of Mr. Craft, was occupied by Jean Baptiste Beaubien'. This project's resident record is Col. Jean Baptiste Beaubien, graded attested, 'J. B. Beaubien, merchant' in the 1833 roster and a licensed trader on the county court's earliest permits. Given name, both middle names and surname agree in full; the rank is this project's addition and the trade agrees. Hurlbut's chapter makes the same succession from Craft to Beaubien and this project already merged the same man there.
merges.does_not_follow: It does not follow that the storehouse is data/structures/jb_beaubien_homestead.json. Hubbard's building is a round-log Fur Company storehouse on the river edge east of a hewn-log house; that identification is a separate argument and this pass does not make it.

merges.rule: Hubbard names 'Billy Caldwell' as the man who drew Shaub-e-nee's annuity for him, who had Shaub-e-nee as his guest at Chicago the evening before Governor Cass's visit in July 1827, and who was camped with his wife near Yellow Head Point in November 1830. This project's resident record is Billy Caldwell (Sauganash), graded attested, born about 1780 and dying at Chicago in 1841. Given name and surname agree exactly; the parenthesis is this project's own gloss of his Potawatomi name and adds nothing to distinguish; and the association with Shaub-e-nee is in both.
merges.does_not_follow: It does not follow that he is placed at Chicago in 1835. The two namings are 1827 and November 1830, and the November 1830 one puts him camped near the Kankakee, not in the town.

merges.rule: Beckwith's footnote at leaf 375 names 'Billy Caldwell, whose name is so intimately connected with early Chicago', as the husband of Min-ne-mung's sister. This project holds the resident Billy Caldwell (Sauganash), graded attested, interpreter to the United States Indian agency at Chicago under Col. T. J. V. Owen and present on the scene date. Billy Caldwell is Billy Caldwell (Sauganash) with the Potawatomi name dropped, which is how the shorter form is always printed; the merge does not rest on the surname, which would be refused, but on the given name plus the surname plus the town - Beckwith says 'early Chicago' and the resident record says Chicago - plus the ROLE, an intermediary between the agency and the Potawatomi, which is exactly the position a marriage into the Yellow Head's family describes. There is no second Billy Caldwell in this project and none in Beckwith.
merges.what_it_adds: A marriage this project did not hold: Caldwell's wife was the sister of Min-ne-mung (the Yellow Head), whose village stood at Yellow-Head's Point north of Momence on the Kankakee. It changes no placement, no grade and no household.

merges.rule: The 1843 directory's post-office history at leaf 419 says the eastern mail was received 'in a one-horse wagon, weekly - John Stephen Coates Hogan, postmaster', in the year after 1832. This project holds the resident John S. C. Hogan, graded attested, whose occupation note reads 'John S. C. Hogan, Postmaster, came in 1832' and whose store is this dataset's hogan_store, 'both a shop and the place where Chicago's mail began'. John Stephen Coates Hogan is John S. C. Hogan written out: three initials in order against three given names in order, S for Stephen, C for Coates, on the same surname, in the same town, in the same OFFICE, in the same years. A three-initial agreement on an uncommon expansion is not a coincidence and this is not a surname merge.
merges.what_it_adds: The expansion of the initials, the man who held the office BEFORE him (Jonathan Nash Bailey, 1832), and the mail's service level year by year across the scene date - which is what the resident record's 'where Chicago's mail began' was missing.

merges.rule: Fergus' Obituary prints the Indian agent as 'Thomas J. Y. Owen', which this project reads as Thomas J. V. Owen — the OCR's Y for V is the commonest single-glyph failure in this whole text and the printed initials are J. V. everywhere else in the corpus. Thomas Jefferson Vance Owen is this project's resident record, and Thomas J. V. Owen is that name initial for initial: J for Jefferson, V for Vance, the same surname, the same office of Indian agent, and the same town. Four things agree and the surname is the least of them. The merge carries a DEATH DATE and nothing else: 15 October 1835.

The 1843 Business Directory advertises 'G. S. Hubbard, forwarding merchant and dealer in produce and provisions' on South Water Street. Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard is this project's resident record and G. S. Hubbard is that name initial for initial, in the same town, in the forwarding trade the resident record already carries. The merge is of the MAN and not of the address: the 1843 frontage is not carried into 1835.

The 1843 alphabetical directory enters 'Gen. Jean Baptiste Beaubien'; this project's resident is Col. Jean Baptiste Beaubien. Three given names and a surname agree exactly and only the militia rank differs, which is what ranks do over eight years. THE RANK IS NOT MERGED WITH THE MAN: this project does not restyle its resident on a directory's authority, and the difference is recorded here rather than smoothed away.

The 1843 Business Directory advertises 'A. Garrett, agent' for two New York insurance companies at Chicago. This project holds Augustus Garrett, a documented auctioneer, and A. Garrett is the same initial and surname in the same town in an agency trade. The merge rests on the initial, the surname, the town and the trade together; the resident record already carries the spelling A. Garrett beside Augustus Garrett, which is the same identification made once before and not a new one.

The 1843 directory's entry for the Chicago Democrat states that its first number was issued on 20 November 1833 by John Calhoun. This project holds a resident John Calhoun, the printer. The spelling is identical, and the merge is RECORDED RATHER THAN ASSUMED so that the next sweep does not have to make it again; what it carries is a founding date for the paper and not an address for the man.

The 1843 Business Directory names the partners of the north-western land agency as William B. Ogden and William E. Jones. This project holds William B. Ogden. The spelling is identical and the merge is recorded rather than assumed; it carries an 1843 office on Kinzie Street and NOTHING about where Ogden was in 1835.

refusals.rule: Hurlbut's opening sentence names the company's Chicago men as 'Hubbard, Beaubien, Crafts and the Kinzies'. 'the Kinzies' is a surname and a plural, and a surname-only merge is always a refusal here however good the rule; the plural makes it worse, because this project holds John Harris Kinzie, James Kinzie and Robert A. Kinzie as three separate residents and the sentence chooses among none of them. Reading 'the Kinzies' as John Harris Kinzie would attach an American Fur Company agency to one named man on the strength of a family plural. Refused.
evidence: data/residents/households/hh_kinzie_john_h.json, hh_kinzie_james.json, hh_kinzie_robert_a.json — three separate Kinzie residents

refusals.rule: The chapter's 'Mr. John Kinzie was not in any business connected with the American Fur Company, but confined himself to his trade, silversmith, making Indian trinkets' is John Kinzie the elder, describing about 1822-23. John Harris Kinzie is his son, a different man, and this project's resident record has him as a forwarding and commission merchant advertising in 1834. The two share a surname and a given name across a generation, which is the standard way early-Chicago sources are misread, and the passage's own date puts its subject in a trade the resident never practised. Refused, and refused loudly: the elder John Kinzie died in 1828 and belongs in no 1835 record at all.
evidence: data/residents/households/hh_kinzie_john_h.json — persons[0], occupation forwarding_and_commission, from his own 1834 advertisement

refusals.rule: The bare surname 'Hubbard' in the chapter's opening list is refused as an identity on its own: a surname-only merge is always a refusal, and this project holds the name Hubbard in more than one place. The man IS Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard, and that is carried by the merge above on the full naming twenty-three lines later — 'Gurdon S. Hubbard, Esq.' — not by this list. The refusal exists so that a later sweep meeting the bare surname finds it already ruled on rather than doing the work again.
evidence: data/research/books/claims/american_fur_company_hurlbut.json bk_afc_001 (the bare surname) and bk_afc_004 (the full naming the merge rests on)

refusals.rule: The bare surname 'Beaubien' in the chapter's opening list is refused for the same reason and with more force than 'Hubbard': this project models Col. Jean Baptiste Beaubien, Madore Beaubien and Mark Beaubien as three separate residents, so a bare Beaubien at Chicago in the fur-trade decades names a family and not a man. The identification is carried by the full naming at bk_afc_008, 'Jean Baptiste Beaubien', and by Hurlbut's own gloss 'The late Col. J.B. Beaubien, of Chicago'.
evidence: data/residents/households/hh_beaubien_jean_baptiste.json, hh_beaubien_madore.json, hh_beaubien_mark.json — three separate Beaubien residents

refusals.rule: Hurlbut says John Crafts 'was a trader sent to Chicago by a Mr. Conant, of Detroit'. This project holds one Conant: Reuben Conant, a name off the post office's letter lists, unplaced, with no trade recorded and his presence on the scene date graded uncertain. Merging Mr. Conant into Reuben Conant would join a surname and nothing else — the source gives no given name at all, and a merge on a bare surname is always a refusal here. It would also join two men the sources put in different towns and fifteen years apart: Hurlbut's Conant is a Detroit merchant of about 1818 who is not said ever to have come to Chicago, and Reuben Conant is a name somebody was writing to AT Chicago by 20 May 1835. Refused.
evidence: data/residents/households/hh_conant_reuben.json — head conant_reuben, division unplaced, present_on_scene_date uncertain

refusals.rule: Hurlbut's bracketed note says William H. Wallace was a Scotchman 'understood to have died in Chicago about 1826'. He is refused against the residents of 1835 as a class, because there is no second spelling to weigh him against: this project holds no Wallace in data/residents/ at all, and a search of the whole of it returns nothing. The refusal is filed rather than left silent so that the next sweep reading this chapter finds William H. Wallace already looked at — a man who died nine years before the scene, whom nothing places in it, and for whom no record was created.
evidence: data/residents/index.json and data/residents/households/ — no Wallace of any spelling

refusals.rule: McIlvaine's list of the town trustees elected on 11 August 1834 names 'John Kinzie'. This project holds John Harris Kinzie, James Kinzie and Robert Allen Kinzie as three separate attested residents, and the elder John Kinzie — the man of Hubbard's own 1818 pages — died in 1828 and cannot be the trustee. So the printed name is impossible for the man it looks like and ambiguous among the men it could be. Reading 'John Kinzie' as John Harris Kinzie would put a dated civic office on one named resident on the strength of a 1911 writer's shortened form of a name three residents share. REFUSED, and the reasoning is the record: the identification is probable and it is not this pass's to make.

Through the 1818 and 1827 narrative Hubbard writes 'Mr. Kinzie' for the head of the house opposite the fort — the man whose long log cabin with a rude piazza he ate breakfast in, and who got on the guard-house roof in a wet blanket. That is the elder John Kinzie, who died in 1828, and this project holds no record for him; John Harris Kinzie is his son and is a different man. 'Mr. Kinzie' is a surname with a courtesy title, which this domain's rule makes a refusal outright. REFUSED.

The trustee list of 11 August 1834 names 'E. Goodrich'. This project holds no Goodrich household at all, and the only Goodrich this project's prose mentions is Grant Goodrich, whose given initial is G and not E. An initial and a surname is surname-only under this domain's rule, and here the one initial that exists disagrees. REFUSED, and recorded so the next sweep does not repeat the search.

McIlvaine quotes 'Mr. E. O. Gale in his Reminiscences of Early Chicago' for the arrival of the brig Illinois on 25 May 1835, with 'himself and brother William with their parents'. This project holds Stephen F. Gale, graded attested. Two initials against a given name and a middle initial, none of them agreeing, on a shared surname. REFUSED. It is worth writing down that the Gale family arrived together in May 1835 by this account, which is a lead on Stephen F. Gale's own arrival and not a merge.

The same passage names Hubbard's informant's 'brother William' — William Gale — among the passengers of 25 May 1835. This project holds Stephen F. Gale, graded attested. William Gale against Stephen F. Gale is a disagreement of given names on a shared surname and is refused for that reason alone, without reaching the middle initial. REFUSED.

The same passage names the family of 'our lamented friend and "oldest citizen," Fernando Jones' among the Illinois's passengers of 25 May 1835. This project holds Benjamin Jones, graded attested. Fernando against Benjamin is a disagreement of given names on a shared surname. REFUSED. Fernando Jones is a real and well-documented early Chicagoan and the refusal here says only that this project does not yet hold him.

The Sunday Times account of the March 1835 purchase names Hubbard's partners as 'Messrs. Russell and Mather'. This project holds a letter-list resident recorded as Russell Janea, graded inferred. 'Russell' alone is a bare surname and a surname-only merge is always a refusal here however good the rule; that the only candidate is itself a letter-list reading of uncertain order makes it worse. REFUSED.

The same account names 'Mather' as the third purchaser and, further down, says the Chicago Historical Society received the plat by gift of 'one of Mr. Mather's descendants, Judge James H. Roberts'. This project holds no Mather. 'Mather' is a bare surname; Judge James H. Roberts is a descendant writing decades later and not the man. REFUSED on both counts, and recorded because a run reading the Russell & Mather addition will meet this name and should meet this note with it.

Hubbard names 'David Hunter' twice — as the Lieut. of the 5th U. S. Infantry commanding Fort Dearborn to 20 May 1831, and as the Major-General who married John Kinzie's youngest daughter Maria. This project holds a letter-list resident recorded as William Hunter, graded inferred. David against William is a disagreement of given names on a shared surname. REFUSED.

Doctor Alexander Wolcott, Indian agent, is named twice in this reading: as the man left in charge of the fort when the troops withdrew in October 1823, and as living in the brick building just within the north stockade in July 1827. THIS PROJECT HOLDS NO WOLCOTT HOUSEHOLD. He is set here against Col. Jean Baptiste Beaubien only because Beaubien is the nearest thing this project has — the other named man occupying a Fort Dearborn building in the 1820s — and the two are plainly different men with different names and different buildings. REFUSED, and recorded as an absence: Wolcott died in 1830 and belongs to the town before the scene.

Hubbard names 'Mrs. Helm' as John Kinzie's eldest daughter, at the 1818 breakfast table and again crying fire from her window in 1827. She is a surname with a courtesy title, which this domain's rule makes a refusal outright, and this project holds no Helm. She is set against Juliette Augusta Magill Kinzie because Juliette is the only attested Kinzie woman this project holds, and the two are different women — Juliette married into the family in 1830, twelve years after this naming. REFUSED.

Hubbard names 'Maria' as John Kinzie's youngest daughter, 'now the wife of Major-General David Hunter'; Maria Kinzie is that name with the family surname the sentence gives her. Set against Juliette Augusta Magill Kinzie, the only Kinzie woman this project holds: Maria Kinzie is a daughter of the house and Juliette Augusta Magill Kinzie married John Harris Kinzie in 1830, so they are a sister and a sister-in-law and not one woman. REFUSED, and this project holds no Maria Kinzie.

Hubbard names Shaub-e-nee repeatedly — welcoming him at Bureau Post, absent from the 1827 payment with his annuity drawn by Caldwell, and going into Big Foot's village alone. He is a single name and this project holds no record for him. He is set against Billy Caldwell (Sauganash) because the two are named in the same sentence and both carry a Potawatomi name beside an English one, which is exactly the kind of pairing a careless sweep would collapse. They are two men and the source says so in one breath. REFUSED.

Hubbard's 1818 building count names 'a cabin on the north side occupied by Antoine Ouilmette'. This project holds no Ouilmette household. He is set against Col. Jean Baptiste Beaubien as the nearest French-Canadian trader household this project holds, and they are different men with different names on different sides of the river. REFUSED, and recorded as an absence rather than a match: the naming is 1818 and nothing here places Ouilmette in 1835.

Hubbard names 'Mr. John Craft', the American Fur Company's agent who erected and occupied the round-log storehouse and after whose death Beaubien occupied it. This project holds no Craft. He is set against Col. Jean Baptiste Beaubien because the two are named as successive occupants of ONE building and a sweep reading the building forward from Beaubien would meet Craft as its previous name; they are two men and the succession is the whole point of the sentence. REFUSED. Hurlbut's chapter names him 'Crafts' with an s and dates his death 'in December, of I think the year 1823'.

The 1843 directory names Jonathan Nash Bailey as the postmaster receiving a weekly horseback mail in 1832. The only Bailey this project holds is Bennet Bailey, a letter-list household graded inferred and unplaced. Jonathan Nash Bailey and Bennet Bailey share a surname and nothing else: the given names are different names, not variant spellings of one, and no initial, trade, address or date connects them. A surname match is a clue and not an identity, and a surname-only merge is always a refusal here. Refused.
refusals.note: Worth a look by a pass that can reach the letter lists themselves: a postmaster is exactly the man whose name appears in a list of uncalled-for letters, and if a Jonathan Bailey is printed in one, this refusal becomes a merge on evidence rather than on hope. It is not one now.

refusals.rule: Schoolcraft's 1821 account, as Beckwith prints it, places the treaty bower 'near the old John Kinzie house' on the north bank. This project holds John Harris Kinzie, attested, forwarding and commission merchant, present on the scene date. John Kinzie is his FATHER, dead in 1828, and the house is the father's; reading John Kinzie as John Harris Kinzie would put a fourteen-year-old boy's father's house under the son's name and would date the son's residence to 1821. The two are separate men with separate records elsewhere in this project, and a shared surname with a shared given name across two generations is the classic trap this file exists to refuse. Refused.
refusals.note: The same refusal covers bk_fer_012's 'Mr. Kinzie's family at the Chicago massacre', which is the elder Kinzie's family in 1812.

refusals.rule: Beckwith's footnote cites 'Mrs. Kinzie's Wau-Iiun' for the Chicago massacre. This project holds Juliette Augusta Magill Kinzie, attested, recorded as the author of Wau-Bun. The work makes the identification obvious and the NAME still does not: Mrs. Kinzie is a courtesy title on a bare surname, and this file refuses a surname-only merge however good the rule, because the project holds three Kinzie households and the honorific chooses among none of them. The citation is recorded on the claim itself, where it belongs; the identity is refused. Refused.
refusals.note: A refusal that costs nothing: nothing in this reading depends on it, because Wau-Bun is already a graded source in this project and Beckwith's footnote adds nothing to it.

refusals.rule: Fergus' Obituary prints 'Spring, Dr., died November 10, 1835' with no given name and no age. This project holds Giles Spring, and T-0423 would put G. Spring's large dwelling-house and fine well on lot 7 of block 16. Dr Spring is a surname and a title, and a surname-only merge is always a refusal here however good the rule; worse, the title disagrees — Giles Spring was a lawyer and this man is a doctor. Reading Dr Spring as Giles Spring would kill off a household inside the scene year on the strength of one surname. Refused, and recorded as a LEAD: if a given name for the doctor is ever found, the date is worth having.

THE VOLUME DISAGREES WITH ITSELF. Its Business Directory names the partners of Bristol & Porter as Robert C. Bristol and Hibbard Porter; its own alphabetical directory, sixty leaves later, enters the same partner as Richard Clark Bristol. Both expand the R. C. Bristol this project holds from the post office's letter lists, and they expand it differently. No reading of one page can settle the other, so neither expansion is adopted and the resident keeps its initials. Refused.

The 1843 Newberry & Dole advertisement lists 'O. Newberry, Detroit' among the transportation line's agents. This project holds Oliver Newberry, and Oliver Newberry of Detroit is who O. Newberry most likely is. IT IS STILL REFUSED, and deliberately: T-0396 is open on which Newberry stood in the firm at Chicago in 1834-35, the corpus reads the partner as Oliver in one year and Walter L. in another, and an 1843 list of a shipping line's out-of-town agents cannot settle an 1835 partnership. Adopting this merge would look like an answer to T-0396 and would not be one.

Newberry & Dole is a firm's own style and George Washington Dole is a man. A style stands for a partnership and names no one member of it; T-0398 records the same fault arriving from the other direction, where a firm's signature was read where a person was wanted. The firm is held as a business and is not merged into either partner. Refused.

The Obituary enters John Kinzie, called Sha-ne-au-kee, Indian agent and trader, dead on 6 January 1828 aged 65. John Harris Kinzie is this project's resident and is the son, alive through the scene year. A death in 1828 at sixty-five cannot be the man the project places in 1835, and the shared given name is exactly the trap a father-and-son pair sets. Refused, against John Harris Kinzie and against James Kinzie and Robert Allen Kinzie with him.

The Obituary has Rev. Jesse Walker dead twelve miles west of Chicago on 5 October 1835; this project holds George E. Walker, a name from the post office's letter lists. The given names disagree outright and only the surname is shared, which is always a refusal here. Refused.

The 1843 directory makes John Wentworth editor and proprietor of the Chicago Democrat; this project holds Elijah Wentworth sen. The given names disagree and only the surname is shared. The refusal matters beyond the surname rule: John Wentworth did not reach Chicago until after the scene year, so no merge on this name may put him in it. Refused.
